title: 2 Samuel 10:1–5
context: When Nahash king of Ammon dies, David sends envoys to comfort his son Hanun, intending to return the kindness Nahash had shown him. Hanun’s princes persuade him that the envoys are spies, so Hanun humiliates them by shaving off half their beards and cutting their garments to expose them. David sends word for the shamed men to wait at Jericho until their beards grow back.

verses.text: After this, the king of the children of Ammon died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Ammon dies, and his son Hanun reigns. Arminian readers note that a change of rulers creates a moment of uncertainty in which relations between neighboring kingdoms can be renewed or broken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the transition as the setting for a test of how Ammon will respond to David’s goodwill. Both traditions read the verse as a brief historical introduction, with the earlier king identified as Nahash in the next verse.

verses.text: David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent by his servants to comfort him concerning his father. David’s servants came into the land of the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes: David plans to show kindness to Hanun as Nahash had shown kindness to him. Arminian readers note that David’s motives are presented as sincere, and that the kindness Nahash showed is not described elsewhere in the text.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repetition of “kindness,” linking this chapter to David’s kindness in chapter 9. Shared ground: both traditions see David acting in good faith, though Nahash had earlier been Saul’s enemy (1 Samuel 11:1–11).

verses.text: But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun their lord, “Do you think that David honors your father, in that he has sent comforters to you? Hasn’t David sent his servants to you to search the city, to spy it out, and to overthrow it?”
verses.arminianNotes: Ammon’s princes tell Hanun that David’s envoys are spies sent to overthrow the city. Arminian readers note how suspicion can twist kindness into a threat, and how the advice of counselors shapes a ruler’s choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the princes’ distrust as leading Hanun into folly that will bring disaster on Ammon. Both traditions read the verse as showing that bad counsel, freely accepted, turns a moment of peace into conflict.

verses.text: So Hanun took David’s servants, shaved off one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks, and sent them away.
verses.arminianNotes: Hanun shaves half of each envoy’s beard and cuts their garments to expose them. Arminian readers see a deliberate insult, meant to humiliate David through his representatives and to reject his offer of friendship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that such treatment of envoys was a grave offense, effectively a declaration of hostility. Shared ground: both traditions read the act as public shaming in a culture where the beard and proper clothing marked dignity.

verses.text: When they told David this, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. The king said, “Wait at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”
verses.arminianNotes: David sends to meet the shamed men and tells them to wait at Jericho until their beards grow back. Arminian readers see David’s care for his servants, sparing them further humiliation before returning to the court.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a king who protects the dignity of those who served him faithfully. Both traditions read the verse as a gentle pastoral response to a painful situation, before David addresses the larger insult from Ammon.
